description: We are Team BladeX and Beyond, comprised of five students and graduates from universities across Canada, South Korea, and Australia, with backgrounds in computer science, engineering, social sciences, and business management. Across borders and time zones, we came together through our shared passion for science, technology, and sustainability. We hope to combine our knowledge, learn from one another, and make open satellite data more accessible and meaningful to people around the world.

details:
What is Harmoniverse?
Harmoniverse is a fire map with a memory. It combines more than 20 years of NASA satellite fire data into one consistent record, so anyone can see how fire has changed in any place on Earth, month by month, since 2003. 

The problem:
Two NASA satellite sensors track fires from space: MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012). VIIRS has sharper eyes, so it counts about six times more fire hotspots than MODIS for the same fires. If you simply join the two records, fire seems to jump sixfold in 2012, even though nothing changed on the ground. As MODIS retires, almost ten years of fire history can no longer be compared fairly with today. 

What we built:

  1. One consistent fire record. We used machine learning to convert the older MODIS years into what VIIRS would have seen. The result is one record of monthly fire activity for every place on Earth, from January 2003 to October 2026.
  2. The Fire Explorer. An interactive web dashboard where anyone can pick a country, city or area on the map and see its fire history as a simple calendar.

How it works:

  1. Collect: We gathered over 400 million fire detections from NASA FIRMS.
  2. Clean: We kept only real vegetation fires and removed things like gas flares and factories.
  3. Organize: We grouped all detections into a grid of 28 km squares, month by month.
  4. Convert: We trained a machine learning model on years when both sensors were working, then used it to convert the older MODIS years to the VIIRS scale.
  5. Test: We checked the model on years it had never seen. Its yearly totals were within 2.0% of the real VIIRS counts.

What you can do with the Fire Explorer:

  • See which months and years had the most fire in your area.
  • Check whether this month is normal or unusual compared with past years.
  • Find the area’s fire season: when it usually starts and peaks.
  • Compare two places or two time periods side by side.
  • Download the data and charts.

Who it helps:

  • Emergency responders and firefighters: know when fire activity in their region is far above normal.
  • Land managers: plan patrols and prescribed burns before the fire season starts.
  • Scientists: study long-term fire trends without the false jump in 2012.
  • Anyone who needs fire history: from students and journalists to local governments and community groups, anyone can explore the fire history of any place on Earth and download the data for free.

Creative Elements:

  • A guided tour. First-time visitors to the Fire Explorer are offered an optional 18-step tour, led by a pixel-art guide, covering the filters, calendar, comparison tools and trend views. Users can go back, skip or exit at any time.
  • Case files from real seasons. Canada 2023, Australia’s Black Summer 2019–20 and Argentina 2020 are told as short case files read straight from the record, each linking to the same view in the Fire Explorer so readers can check the story themselves.
  • The Fire Story. Any area and season can be exported as a plain-language summary that anyone can read and share, without needing to interpret a chart.
  • A retro desktop look. Every chart opens in its own old-school computer window, like “FireMap.exe” or “Harmonize.exe,” which makes complex satellite data feel friendly and fun to explore.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML and CSS
  • Data processing: pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas and Shapely (country and province labels), PyArrow (Parquet files), and h5py, pyhdf and netCDF4 (reading GFED regions, MODIS land cover and GFED5 burned-area files)
  • Machine learning: LightGBM, with separate day and night models; LightGBM in random-forest mode served as a comparison
  • Web platform and visualization: plain JavaScript with no framework; all maps and charts are drawn by our own code on HTML canvas, without chart or map libraries
  • Analysis charts: Matplotlib
  • Testing: pytest
  • Design: Figma
  • Development tools: Cursor, Git, GitHub and Claude Code
  • Hosting: Vercel

How We Used SI/AI:
We designed the layout, colours, visual style and character concepts ourselves in Figma, chose the methods, and ran and checked every experiment. SI/AI tools supported specific tasks:

  • Code: Claude Code and Cursor helped write and debug the data pipeline, experiments and web platform. All code was guided, reviewed and tested by the team.
  • Research and writing: ChatGPT and Claude helped us find and summarise research papers, and draft and edit the project report and website text. We checked every source, number and claim ourselves. (We tested our own hypothesis)
  • Pixel-art characters: we created the five character concepts. Claude, used through Figma, generated first drafts from our brief; we then edited and refined them and decided on the final designs.
  • Prototypes: Claude Artifacts turned our Figma designs into HTML prototypes, used as the visual reference for the final interface.
  • Design touch-ups: Figma’s SI/AI agent made minor alignment and spacing corrections.

All SI/AI output was reviewed before use.
